paras: The attempted lynching of Mike Rourke took place on January 14, 1881, at Tombstone, Arizona Territory, when a mob tried to hang Rourke, a young man arrested for shooting P. Schneider, chief engineer of the Tombstone Mill and Mining Company, at nearby Charleston. Officers kept the prisoner from the crowd and took him under armed guard to the jail at Tucson, where he awaited examination and from which he escaped in April. The Omaha Daily Bee instead reported that the killer, "John Call," was taken from jail and hanged by a mob.

Schneider was shot about midday on Friday, January 14, at the corner of a corral near the eating house at Charleston, as he walked toward the mill. The man who fired was a young miner known as "Johnny behind the deuce," whom the Arizona Weekly Citizen named as P. or Mike Rourke and who gave his age as "nineteen next April."

According to the account telegraphed from Charleston, the two men had words at the table, after which Rourke armed himself, waited at the corral, and shot Schneider through the head while Schneider asked to be let alone. Rourke gave the Citizen a different account, saying that Schneider had insulted him, followed him to the corral and crowded him with a knife in his hand before he drew and fired. Constable George McKelvey caught Rourke near the river and drove him toward Tombstone, nearly overtaken by pursuers.

At Tombstone Rourke was put under guard at Jim Vogan's saloon, where, in the Citizen's words, "a mob collected and would undoubtedly have hung the prisoner but for the firmness of Marshal Sippy and the other officers." Rourke said his captors had told him they would hold an inquest on Schneider and, if he had killed him, "would hang me in twenty minutes." Sippy and Deputy Sheriff Behan then drove off with Rourke between them, escorted for twelve miles by fifteen riflemen, amid threats that "angry vigilantes" would board the train at Pantano. He reached the Tucson jail in the charge of Marshal Sippy and Constables Westfuller, Virgil Earp and George McKelvey.

Rourke's examination for the killing was set before Judge Neugass, together with that of Robert Petty, charged with being an accessory before the act. A letter from a Charleston resident dated January 22 said the pistol belonged to Petty and that people there regarded the shooting as "an unprovoked and most cruel murder." No report of the result of the examination or of a trial appears in the coverage. In April the Daily Los Angeles Herald, citing the Tucson Journal, reported that O'Rourke had escaped from the Tucson jail by scaling the sixteen-foot wall of the yard.

The Arizona Weekly Citizen of Tucson covered the case most fully, with a headline announcing that "Rourke Narrowly Escapes Lynching" over the Charleston telegram and Rourke's own statement, presented as "Two Conflicting Reports." A week later the paper said the evidence supported Rourke's story, mocked papers that had "called loudly for the prisoner's gore," naming the Tombstone Epitaph, and credited Virgil Earp and his companions with saving him "from the fury of the miners." Even so, it said a dozen men in the county jail deserved lynching "much more than does young Rourke," and it later printed the Charleston letter saying the prisoner had "escaped what he richly deserved."

Outside the territory, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union ran the first dispatch under the headline "A Cowardly Murder." A Tucson letter in the Daily Los Angeles Herald described the killer as "a mere boy" in a "carnival of murder" and recommended "a summary way of disposing of this class." The Phoenix Herald reprinted the Citizen's one-sentence summary, while the Omaha Daily Bee's territorial column carried the report of a hanging.

The Omaha Daily Bee's version, which named the killer "John Call" and said he was hanged five hours later, conflicts with the Tucson reports, which were closer to the events and show Rourke alive in jail a week later and escaping three months afterward. The Citizen first credited Marshal Sippy and Deputy Sheriff Behan with saving him and later Virgil Earp and his companions.

bases: A mob at Tombstone tried to seize and hang a prisoner accused of murder but was held off by officers, an attempted lynching (A2, A4, A10).

A mob acting on the murder accusation tried to hang Rourke, but the Arizona reports show him delivered alive to the Tucson jail, awaiting examination, and escaping in April (A3, A4, A8, A11); only the distant Omaha Bee says he was hanged (A6).
Three Tucson reports agree that a mob tried and failed to hang Rourke (A2, A4, A7, A10), while the Omaha Daily Bee says the killer was taken from jail and hanged (A6).
